## Setup and Data Loading

```{r}
#| include: false

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(gt)

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Load the training and test datasets
ems_train <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_train.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

ems_test <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_test.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Check the structure of the training data
glimpse(ems_train)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Check the training and test periods
ems_train |>
  summarise(
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Weeks = n_distinct(Week)
  )

ems_test |>
  summarise(
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Weeks = n_distinct(Week)
  )

```

## 1. Response-Time Trends

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Plot weekly response times by emergency category
ggplot(ems_train, aes(
  x = Week,
  y = Arrival_Seconds,
  color = Category
)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly EMS Response Times by Emergency Category",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)",
    color = "Emergency Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

**Interpretation.** On average, response times were shorter for life-threatening incidents at 596 seconds while non-life-threatening incidents averaged 896 seconds. Non-life-threatening response times were also more variable.

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate mean response time by category
ems_train |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Mean_Arrival_Seconds = round(
      mean(Arrival_Seconds, na.rm = TRUE),
      2
    )
  )

```

## 2. Seasonality and Unusual Changes

```{r}
#| include: false

# Convert training data to a weekly time series (tsibble)
ems_train_ts <- ems_train |>
  as_tsibble(
    key = Category,
    index = Week
  )

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Examine seasonal patterns in arrival times
ems_train_ts |>
  gg_season(Arrival_Seconds, period = "year") +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern of EMS Response Times",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate trend and seasonal strength
stl_features <- ems_train_ts |>
  features(
    Arrival_Seconds,
    feat_stl,
    .period = 52
  )

stl_features |>
  select(
    Category,
    trend_strength,
    seasonal_strength_52
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
  )

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Identify weeks with the highest response times
ems_train |>
  arrange(desc(Arrival_Seconds)) |>
  select(
    Week,
    Category,
    Arrival_Seconds,
    Incidents
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

```

**Interpretation.** Response times showed stronger long-term trends than seasonal patterns during the training period (2013–2025). Annual seasonal strength was 0.223 for life-threatening emergencies and 0.260 for non-life-threatening emergencies. Non-life-threatening incidents also experienced larger unusual response-time spikes, particularly during 2020.

## 3. Response-Time Forecasting Models

```{r}
#| include: false

# Convert test data to a weekly tsibble
ems_test_ts <- ems_test |>
  as_tsibble(
    key = Category,
    index = Week
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Fit response-time forecasting models: Seasonal Naive, ETS and ARIMA
response_models <- ems_train_ts |>
  model(
    Seasonal_Naive = SNAIVE(Arrival_Seconds ~ lag("year")),
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds),
    ARIMA = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Forecasts response times for the 52-week test period
response_fc <- response_models |>
  forecast(new_data = ems_test_ts)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Compare forecast model accuracy on the test data
response_accuracy <- response_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_test_ts) |>
  select(
    Category,
    .model,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE
  ) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

response_accuracy

```

### Manual ARIMA Model Selection

```{r}
# Check differencing requirements for each emergency category

ems_train_ts |>
  features(Arrival_Seconds, unitroot_ndiffs)

ems_train_ts |>
  features(Arrival_Seconds, unitroot_nsdiffs)
```

```{r}
# ACF and PACF: Life-Threatening emergencies

ems_train_ts |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  mutate(
    diff_arrival = difference(Arrival_Seconds)
  ) |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    diff_arrival,
    plot_type = "partial"
  )
```

```{r}
# ACF and PACF: Non-Life-Threatening emergencies

ems_train_ts |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  mutate(
    diff_arrival = difference(Arrival_Seconds)
  ) |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    diff_arrival,
    plot_type = "partial"
  )
```

```{r}
# Manual versus automatic ARIMA model comparison
# Models fitted using training data only

manual_response_fit <- ems_train_ts |>
  model(
    ARIMA_011 = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds ~ pdq(0, 1, 1)),
    ARIMA_012 = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds ~ pdq(0, 1, 2)),
    Auto_ARIMA = ARIMA(Arrival_Seconds),
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

# Compare model fit using training-data AICc
manual_response_fit |>
  glance() |>
  select(Category, .model, AICc) |>
  arrange(Category, AICc)
```

```{r}
# Evaluate manual ARIMA, automatic ARIMA, and ETS
# Using the same 52-week test period

manual_response_fc <- manual_response_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = ems_test_ts)

manual_response_accuracy <- manual_response_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_test_ts) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(Category, RMSE)

manual_response_accuracy
```

### Manual vs. Automatic ARIMA Interpretation

Manual ARIMA models were selected using differencing tests and the ACF/PACF patterns of the training series. Both emergency categories suggested one regular difference and no seasonal difference. ARIMA(0,1,1) and ARIMA(0,1,2) were compared with automatically selected ARIMA and ETS models using the same 52-week test period.

ETS achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE for both emergency categories. However, manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved the lowest MAPE, with 8.37% for life-threatening emergencies and 19.02% for non-life-threatening emergencies. Manual ARIMA(0,1,1) also outperformed automatic ARIMA across all three test accuracy metrics.

Although automatic ARIMA had the lowest AICc among the ARIMA candidates on the training data, it produced higher test-set errors than the manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) model. These findings demonstrate that automatically selected models do not always provide the most accurate forecasts on unseen data, and model selection depends partly on the evaluation metric.

```{r}
#| echo: false

# ETS forecasts of EMS Response Times
ets_fc <- response_fc |>
  filter(.model == "ETS")

# Show recent history, ETS forecasts, and actual test values
ets_fc |>
  autoplot(
    ems_train_ts |>
      filter(Week >= as.Date("2023-01-01")),
    level = c(80, 95)
  ) +
  autolayer(
    ems_test_ts,
    Arrival_Seconds,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Category,
    scales = "free_y",
    ncol = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "ETS Forecasts of EMS Response Times",
    subtitle = "Forecasts compared with actual response times in the 52-week test period",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

**Interpretation.** ETS achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE for both emergency categories in the expanded model comparison. However, manual ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved slightly lower MAPE. Both models forecasted life-threatening response times more accurately than non-life-threatening response times.

```{r}
# Check residuals for ETS and ARIMA models
# ETS residual diagnostics: Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ETS) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# ETS residual diagnostics: Non-Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ETS) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# ARIMA residual diagnostics: Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ARIMA) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# ARIMA residual diagnostics: Non-Life-Threatening emergencies

response_models |>
  filter(Category == "Non-Life-Threatening") |>
  select(ARIMA) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
# Ljung-Box test for response-time model residuals

response_models |>
  select(ETS, ARIMA) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 20)
```

### Residual Diagnostics Interpretation

The Ljung–Box test was conducted at lag 20 to evaluate residual autocorrelation. ARIMA showed no statistically significant remaining autocorrelation for either life-threatening (p = 0.966) or non-life-threatening (p = 0.996) emergencies. In contrast, ETS showed significant remaining autocorrelation for both life-threatening (p = 0.031) and non-life-threatening (p = 0.041) emergencies.

Although automatically selected ARIMA demonstrated more favorable residual diagnostics, ETS achieved lower RMSE and MAE on the 52-week test set. Manual ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved slightly lower MAPE than ETS. These findings suggest that model selection should consider forecast accuracy, the evaluation metric, and residual diagnostics rather than relying on a single measure.

## 3.1. Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Run rolling-origin cross-validation for the ETS model
response_cv <- ems_train_ts |>
  stretch_tsibble(
    .init = 260,
    .step = 13
  )

response_cv_fit <- response_cv |>
  model(
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

response_cv_fc <- response_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

response_cv_accuracy <- response_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(
    ems_train_ts,
    by = c("Category", ".model")
  ) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE)

response_cv_accuracy

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Calculate forecast errors for each CV period
response_cv_results <- response_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(
    ems_train_ts |>
      as_tibble() |>
      select(
        Week,
        Category,
        Actual = Arrival_Seconds
      ),
    by = c("Week", "Category")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Error = Actual - .mean,
    Absolute_Error = abs(Error),
    APE = abs(Error / Actual) * 100
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Keep valid cross-validation results
response_cv_results_valid <- response_cv_results |>
  filter(
    !is.na(Actual),
    is.finite(APE)
  )

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Plot rolling-origin forecast errors over time
response_cv_results_valid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Week, y = APE, color = Category)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Category,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation of EMS Response Times",
    subtitle = "One-week-ahead ETS forecast errors across 28 forecast periods",
    x = "Forecast Week",
    y = "Absolute Percentage Error (%)",
    color = "Emergency Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )

```

**Interpretation.** Rolling-origin validation showed that ETS performed well across different periods. Forecast errors stayed low for life-threatening incidents with a MAPE of 3.19% compared to 7.38%.

## 3.2 Full History vs. Recent Training Window

```{r}
#| include: false

# Create the 2022-onward training dataset
response_train_recent <- ems_train_ts |>
  filter(Week >= as.Date("2022-01-01"))

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Fit ETS using the recent training period
response_recent_fit <- response_train_recent |>
  model(
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

```

```{r}
#| include: false

# Forecast the test period using the recent-history ETS model
response_recent_fc <- response_recent_fit |>
  forecast(new_data = ems_test_ts)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate recent-history ETS forecast accuracy
response_recent_accuracy <- response_recent_fc |>
  accuracy(ems_test_ts) |>
  select(Category, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Compare full-history and recent-history ETS accuracy
response_window_accuracy <- bind_rows(
  response_accuracy |>
    filter(.model == "ETS") |>
    mutate(Training_Window = "Full History (2013-2025)"),
  
  response_recent_accuracy |>
    mutate(Training_Window = "Recent History (2022-2025)")
) |>
  select(
    Category,
    Training_Window,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE
  )

response_window_accuracy |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "ETS Response-Time Accuracy by Training Window",
    subtitle = "Life-Threatening vs. Non-Life-Threatening EMS Incidents"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    Category = "Emergency Category",
    Training_Window = "Training Window",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    MAE = "MAE",
    MAPE = "MAPE"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(RMSE, MAE),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = MAPE,
    decimals = 2,
    pattern = "{x}%"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = everything()
  )

```

**Interpretation.** Full-history training produced lower RMSE for both emergency categories. However, recent-history training slightly improved MAPE for non-life-threatening emergencies (18.79% versus 19.79%). Overall, the results were mixed, with no consistent advantage from using only recent data.

## 4. Incident Counts and Response Times

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Plot the relationship between incident volume and response time
ggplot(
  ems_train,
  aes(
    x = Incidents,
    y = Arrival_Seconds,
    color = Category
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Category,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Incident Counts and EMS Response Times",
    subtitle = "Weekly observations from the training period",
    x = "Weekly Incident Count",
    y = "Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate the correlation by emergency category
incident_correlations <- ems_train |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Correlation = cor(
      Incidents,
      Arrival_Seconds,
      use = "complete.obs"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Correlation = round(Correlation, 3)
  )

incident_correlations

```

**Interpretation.** Higher incident volume was associated with longer response times for life-threatening incidents (r = 0.501). The relationship was weaker for non-life-threatening incidents (r = 0.233).

## 5. Future EMS Response-Time Forecasts

```{r}
# Prepare all available response-time data
# Combine training and testing observations

response_full <- bind_rows(ems_train, ems_test) |>
  arrange(Category, Week) |>
  select(Week, Category, Arrival_Seconds) |>
  as_tsibble(key = Category, index = Week)

# Refit ETS models using all available historical data
future_response_models <- response_full |>
  model(
    ETS = ETS(Arrival_Seconds)
  )

# Display fitted models
future_response_models
```

```{r}
# Forecast EMS response times for the next 52 weeks
# The first 4 weeks represent the short-term forecast

future_response_fc <- future_response_models |>
  forecast(h = 52, level = c(80, 95))

# Display the first 4 forecast weeks for each category
future_response_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  slice_head(n = 4) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    Forecast_Minutes = .mean / 60
  ) |>
  select(
    Week,
    Category,
    Forecast_Seconds = .mean,
    Forecast_Minutes
  )
```

```{r}
# Future EMS response-time forecasts
# Display historical observations and 80%/95% prediction intervals

future_response_fc |>
  autoplot(
    response_full |> filter_index("2024 Jan" ~ .),
    level = c(80, 95)
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Category, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "NYC EMS Response-Time Forecasts: 52 Weeks Ahead",
    subtitle = "ETS models with 80% and 95% prediction intervals",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Average Call-to-Arrival Time (Seconds)"
  )
```

### Future Response-Time Forecast Interpretation

Using all available observations through September 14, 2026, ETS models forecasted average weekly call-to-arrival times of approximately 15.53 minutes for life-threatening emergencies and 43.48 minutes for non-life-threatening emergencies. These forecasts reflect the elevated response times observed toward the end of the historical period.

Both ETS models projected relatively constant response times across the 52-week horizon. However, the 80% and 95% prediction intervals widened substantially, indicating greater uncertainty over longer forecasting periods.

The non-life-threatening forecast intervals extended below zero at longer horizons, which is not physically meaningful for response times. This highlights a limitation of the model's uncertainty estimates and suggests that longer-term forecasts should be interpreted cautiously.

Overall, these forecasts could help identify potential response-time pressures for EMS planning, but they should not be treated as exact predictions. Unexpected operational changes and external disruptions could substantially affect actual response times.

## 6. Response-Time Results

**Takeaway.** Life-threatening emergencies generally had shorter and more consistent call-to-arrival times than non-life-threatening emergencies.

On the 52-week test set, ETS achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE for both emergency categories. However, manually selected ARIMA(0,1,1) achieved the lowest MAPE, with 8.37% for life-threatening emergencies and 19.02% for non-life-threatening emergencies. The manual model also outperformed automatically selected ARIMA across all three accuracy measures, demonstrating the value of comparing manual and automatic model specifications.

Rolling-origin cross-validation showed relatively low one-week-ahead ETS forecast errors. Residual diagnostics identified some remaining autocorrelation in the ETS models, while training-window comparisons produced mixed results.

Using all available data through September 14, 2026, the refitted ETS models projected average call-to-arrival times of approximately 15.53 minutes for life-threatening emergencies and 43.48 minutes for non-life-threatening emergencies. These forecasts reflected elevated response times near the end of the historical period.

Although these predictions could help NYC EMS anticipate potential response-time pressures, uncertainty increased considerably across the 52-week forecast horizon. The non-life-threatening prediction intervals also extended below zero, highlighting limitations in the model's uncertainty estimates. Therefore, forecasts should be interpreted cautiously and used as planning aids rather than exact predictions.
